blocks.p: Lesson card from the catechism, the infant school on the garden ring, Abundance.

Why do children not cry? Because there is nothing in all the worlds to make them. If a friend falls down and says strange words, what do we do? Cover the little ones’ ears, and call the Mercy Office. Is it passed by touch? No. By the words. Where does our friend go? Up, to be made well. When may we visit? Healing takes the time it takes.
On Mars the dawn came up blue, and the great dome of Abundance had been built to make it gold.

Sol Tarren liked to be awake for it. He stood at the window of the bishop’s residence and watched the change come down the curve of the glass. Beyond the dome the sky was the thin, cold blue of a Martian morning, and the sun rose into it small and pale, like a coin let fall into water. Then the panels of the vault took that light and warmed it, until the whole sky over the city was the color of honey held up to a lamp. What came down into the streets was not the light of Mars at all. It was better.

Abundance woke under it. The lamps of the farm ring went from violet to white. The first tram slid out along the outer rail with a soft, drawn sigh. Far down the dome, on the tiers of the Bounty Market, the awnings went up one after another like flowers opening along a stem, and the music began, so softly that no one could ever have said which note had been the first. Then the cathedral rang the first office over his head, and in every house in the city a Pearl brightened as someone knelt down before it.

In all that waking city there was no one sick and no one poor, and no one who would ever have to stand at a grave. He had spent four hundred years telling people that a gift was meant to be enjoyed, and he saw no reason to make an exception of himself.

He washed in cold water, which he preferred and Pell deplored. In the glass was the face he had worn since the Judgment, lean and composed and about forty, with lines at the eyes that never deepened, because every autumn they were smoothed away. Renewal had taken every mark four centuries had made on him but one: a thin shining scar across the base of his left thumb, the kind a burn leaves when it has been let heal on its own. He did not know how he had come by it. The hood had passed it over cycle after cycle, and he had never asked why. It did not seem the sort of thing one asked. When he thought of it at all, he thought of it as a kind of signature: the one place on his body that was still exactly as he had left it.
Pell had laid the stoles in the top drawer of the wardrobe, as he did in every lodging, and at the back of the drawer, where Pell always put it, lay the rule.

It was a flat bar of steel no longer than his hand, dull with handling, and along one edge it was marked in the old measure of the archive drawings: inches, cut down into halves and quarters and eighths and sixteenths by lines so fine that he had to tilt it to the window to see them. It had been among his things longer than Pell had, which was sixty years, and Sol could not think why a bishop would own it. He had nothing to measure. Twice he had set it out for reclamation, and twice he had gone back for it before the day was out, and after the second time he had stopped trying. Instead he had taken to picking it up when he had something to think about. His thumb went along the cut edge of its markings by itself, the way a tongue goes to a tooth.
He was holding it when Pell, his deacon, came in with the tea, pressed and shaved and pleased as always to find the day waiting for him. Beside the pot stood a small stoneware jar.

“Honey, Your Grace, from the farm ring. They keep real bees there, under the lamps. I asked at the Pearl last night, and it was on the step this morning.” He poured. “And the cathedral asks whether you would preside tomorrow. A cargo tram came off the outer rail yesterday, below the eastern ring, and went through a platform. One woman, a Liesel Varga. The family has asked for a bishop, if there’s one in the colony.”
“Of course,” Sol said. He liked to be asked for. He liked it, if he was honest, rather more than a bishop should.
“And His Holiness’s office sends its regards.” Pell’s voice warmed a little on the title, as everyone’s did. “They say he asked after you at table.”

Sol kept his face as it was, which took some doing. Ascensions had been failing in the inner colonies since the spring, a few here and a few there, and of all the bishops of Life the Hierarch had asked for Tarren, because Tarren was the one who came back with a tidy answer. Everyone said so. Sol had heard it said in corridors by men who thought he was out of earshot, and he had never gone back to correct them.

“The precentor sent word too, after you’d retired.” Pell’s pleasant face became, for a moment, delicate. “One of the failures here is theirs. A cantor, Ilse Dorn. She fell from the north gallery in the summer, at a rehearsal, and she didn’t...” He made a small, neat gesture, as a man brushes a crumb from a cloth. “She didn’t go through. The choir has been told it’s a technical delay. He wonders whether you’d say something to them.”
“How are they taking it?”
“Very well, he says. Only the children in the choir keep asking when she’s coming back.” Pell considered it. “Not upset, he says. Only asking.”
Then Pell went up to the administrator’s registry for the records Sol had asked for, and they agreed to meet at the market at noon. Sol would walk. He always walked in Abundance.

When the door had closed he sat on at the window with the tea and the rule, and thought about a woman who had sung from a gallery for a hundred years and then fallen out of it, and about children who kept asking. There would be an answer. There always was. A small pressure had come behind his left eye, as it had been coming lately, now and then, and he closed his eyes against the brightness of the dome.
His tea was cold.

A skin had come up on it, and the honey had sunk to the bottom in a pale thread. The little brass clock on the mantel said eighteen minutes to the hour. Pell had gone out on the half hour; Sol had heard the chime under the closing of the door. Twelve minutes. He had not slept. He went back over them the way he would have gone back through a sermon for a lost page, and there was nothing in them at all: not a thought, not a sound, not the cup going cold under his hand.
The rule lay on the cloth in front of him, squared exactly to the edge of the table, as if he had been measuring something. He did not remember putting it down.

He put it back behind the stoles, and took out the gold one for the season, and settled it on his shoulders in the glass. The pressure had gone. He was due in the east hall in the autumn, and whatever this was, the hood would find it and set it right with everything else. He did not mention it to Pell. After a while he did not mention it to himself.

The residence stood on a little square below the cathedral, around a fountain of red stone that the children of the square ran through every morning on the way to their lessons. This morning it was dry. A few children stood at the rim looking at the still water, and their parents behind them with the patient faces of people who have asked at the Pearl and been told a thing will be seen to.
The smallest, a girl of four or five with her hair in two tight knots, had climbed onto the wet rim to see better. Her boots went out from under her, and she came down hard on her knees on the stone.

Sol reached her before her mother did. He knelt on the wet paving, which would do nothing for his robe, and set her on her feet. There was a bright bead of blood on one knee. She looked down at it with grave interest, the way a child looks at a beetle she has turned over, and then up at him.
“Look,” she said.
“I see. That’s a very fine scrape. You’ll want to show it to everyone.”

She nodded and went to show her mother. She had not cried. It came to him, watching her go, that he could not remember when he had last heard a child cry: not here, not anywhere, not in any year he could have put a number to. There was nothing in all the worlds to make them. It was one of the first blessings and one of the least remarked, and he stood a moment in the square and remarked it, and gave thanks.

Then he was kneeling at the foot of the basin, where a small brass plate was let into the stone, and he had it open with his thumbnail before he knew that he meant to. Inside sat the valve, a little wheel on a bronze body furred green with scale. It was stiff, as he had known it would be. He did not turn it open. He turned it a quarter turn shut, against itself, and felt the scale crack and give; then he struck the body once with the heel of his hand, just below the stem, and opened it.

The jet coughed, spat, and leapt. In the light pull of Mars it went up nearly three times as high as it would have gone on Earth and came down slowly, in long glittering ropes, and the children shrieked and ran through it with their arms out.
“Your Grace! Where did you learn to do that?”

He did not know. His hands had known which way the wheel wanted to go first, and they had not told him how. “I have a fountain at home in Concord,” he said, getting to his feet, “that I’ve been quarreling with for a hundred years. One picks up its habits.”

They laughed. “The Pearl sent us a bishop,” a man said, and a woman said, “Well, I did ask,” and Sol laughed with them. He went out of the square with his knees soaked through and the old scar on his thumb shining wet, pleased with himself for the whole length of the next street, and not much minding that it showed.

The garden ring curved away under the dome in a long slope of lawns and fruit walls. Its houses stood open to the morning, their front rooms folded back onto the grass, and at the back of each a Pearl glowed in its alcove like a hearth. Families were at breakfast. Sol liked to see it: the tables carried out under the lamps, and at the end of every table, pushed right up to the gold, a place laid for someone who was not in the room.

At one house the Pearl held no one. It showed only a soft, even light, paler than its neighbors’, and the family ate facing it as contentedly as anyone on the ring. Their son was in Mercy, the mother told him when she saw him look: resting in the City while the Face healed him, not yet well enough for visits. They kept his place all the same. Sol blessed the light for her. He had passed a great many resting lights in his life, and it came to him, going on, that he had never seen one wake. Healing took the time it took. It was like the City to be patient.
At the next gate there were white ribbons, and on the path, in a child’s chalk letters a foot high, BON VOYAGE GRANDPA. Neighbors were drifting in with covered dishes.
“Your Grace!” A woman was already on her feet at the table. “Oh, would you? Mother will never forgive us if she hears you went by.”
He went up the path. The family made room for him, but Sol was looking at the Pearl.

The table ran right up into the alcove, and in the gold it went on. It ran away into the light, longer than the house, longer than the garden ring, heaped with fruit and bread and pale cakes, and people sat at it all the way along, young and in white, eating and laughing and reaching. At the near end, so close that she might have been sitting at the family’s own table, a young woman in white was buttering a roll. She looked up and saw him and set it down.
“Is that Bishop Tarren? Liv, why didn’t you say? Bring him where I can see him.”
“Nessa Amsel,” Sol said, and bowed to the Pearl. “The cathedral was full of white lilies.”
She clapped her hands. “Ninety-one years, and he remembers the lilies!”
He had ascended her himself, on his second visit to Abundance. He remembered nearly all of them, and he had never stopped being pleased when it showed.

“Emmet’s coming up this afternoon,” Nessa said. “He came off the glazing gantry two nights ago, the great fool. A hundred and sixty years up and down this dome, and never once fell off it till now.” She patted the bench beside her, where a place had been laid and a cup filled. “I’ve saved him the seat. Tell whoever has him to be quick about it, Your Grace. And tell him, when he comes through, not to look back at the gate. Tell him to look at me.” For a moment her hand lay still on the bench. “The bread is very good today.”

“Grandma’s always eating,” said Liv’s small daughter, and Nessa said, “Well, there’s always more,” and picked up her roll to prove it, and they all laughed. The children had never had a morning without her, and they would never in their lives have to lose anyone at all.

Liv cut him a slice of the farewell cake, iced white in the shape of the pearl gate, and wrapped it in a napkin and would not hear of his refusing. “Tonight we’ll have them both at supper,” she said, and her face shone. “Together at the end of the table, after ninety-one years. Isn’t it a mercy?”
“It is,” Sol said, and meant it with his whole heart.
He ate the cake as he walked, like a boy let out of lessons, and found himself wondering, as he did now and then, whom he would visit, if he were the kind of man who visited.

There was no one. He went through the Pearls a dozen times a year, for the bereaved and the newly ascended, and never once on his own account, because there was no one in all the City of the Throne whom he had lost. In four hundred years he had lost no one. Or he could not remember losing anyone, which in a man of his age, he supposed, came to the same thing. He had sent up more souls than any bishop in the colonies, and could have named most of them, and not one of them would have laid a place for him.

He did not let himself mind. Only, no one alive had known him young. Even Aurelian, who had renewed beside him every cycle since their ordination, had met him already a priest. Whatever young man had once stood in his shoes and answered to his name, there was no one left in all the worlds who could have told him what that man was like, and until this moment, with cake on his fingers, he had never thought to wonder.

At the end of the ring the old Founders’ Walk ran off toward the cathedral, straight and broad, paved in the first red stone the colony had ever cut. It was the shortest way. It was lit and swept, its fountains ran, nothing in Abundance forbade it, and there was no one in it. There never was. Sol glanced down its long gold emptiness, as he always did, and turned the other way, as he always did, and went round by the farm terraces; and he was halfway along them, among the vines and the white hives, before he noticed that he had done it again. The terraces were prettier, he supposed. The rest of Abundance seemed to think so too, which pleased him obscurely, as if the whole colony shared a private taste of his.

The banners had gone up in the night. They hung the whole height of the cathedral’s red flank, white and gold, and each bore the same words in letters taller than a man: Behold, I make all things new. The autumn Renewal had begun.

Abundance kept it as a festival: honey cakes on trays at every corner, ribbons on the trams, and on the cathedral steps a band of fiddles and horns, so that for once the music came from somewhere. The line for the Renewal chapel ran down the steps and twice around the square. People had come before the dome turned gold to stand in it, with stools and flasks and children on their shoulders, and they stood in the light laughing, the way people laugh in a line for something they know will be wonderful. A big man near the front was telling everyone that he had been there since the dark and would not give up his place for his own mother, and his mother, who looked no older than he did, laughed louder than anyone.

From the chapel’s far door the renewed were coming out, one at a time, a little unsteady on their feet, blinking like swimmers come up out of a deep, cool pool, into the arms of friends with cakes. Every one of them looked younger than the face that had gone in, and lighter; there was no other word for it. A woman came down the steps with her arms flung wide and called out, “I feel as if I’ve put down something heavy, and I can’t think what it was!” and the whole square laughed with her.

Then someone in the line saw him, and the quiet went down the line ahead of him like wind through grass. The bishop. It’s Bishop Tarren. After the responses in a full cathedral it was the sound he liked best in all the worlds, and somewhere in the last century or two he had stopped pretending to himself that he didn’t. They asked for him by name, and he gave them theirs back.

Near the chapel doors a young man stood by himself, very pale, holding his hands together as if he were afraid of what they might do. A first life, Sol saw at once: forty years old in fact as well as in face, and this his first time. Sol sat down on the step beside him, robes and all.
“Your first?”
“Yes, Your Grace. I know it’s foolish.”
“It isn’t foolish. What’s your name?”
“Corran.”

“Corran. You’ll lie down, and they’ll bring the hood down over you, and it will be warm, like sitting in the sun with your eyes shut. When you wake you’ll feel as though someone had opened a window in a room you didn’t know was close. You’ll still be you. Only lighter.”
“What will they take?”
“Only what’s been heavy. Whatever you’d have put down yourself, if you’d known how.”
“But how will I know what it was?”
Sol smiled at him. “You won’t,” he said. “That’s the gift.”

The fear went out of the young man’s shoulders all at once, the way it went out of people when Sol talked to them. Sol laid a hand on his head and blessed him. The people near them had gone quiet to watch, and he knew they were watching, and did it well.

In the corner of his own sight, small and gold, his Halo had marked the opening of the season: The autumn Renewal. Sion, the east hall. His place was near the end of it, in the good chairs beside Aurelian’s, and afterward the two of them would sit on the steps of the east hall with a tray of honey cakes between them, as they had every cycle for longer than most of this square had been alive.
And tonight there would be the residence.

He thought of it in the noise of the square the way one thinks of a stair in the dark that may or may not have one more step. Pell would make his small requests at the Pearl and go to bed, and the house would be silent: a silence so even and so deep that he sometimes thought it less an absence of sound than something laid down under everything, to stand on. He would sit in it with a book until the lamps dimmed, and nothing would need him. He had never let himself decide whether that was the best hour of his day or something else, and he did not decide it now.
The cathedral rang noon over the square, and the band on the steps stopped playing to let it ring.

Below the cathedral the great stair went down into the Bounty Market. Pell would be somewhere at the bottom of it with the morning’s tablets, and after that would come the administrator, and the failures, and in a day or a week the tidy answer, as there always was. Sol brushed the last of the cake from his fingers and went down into the gold, smiling, among ten thousand faces, and every one of them was young.
